facts.claim: About three quarters of Asch participants conformed to an obviously wrong unanimous line judgment at least once.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because unanimity created informational doubt and social pressure even when the private visual answer was clear.
facts.whyWrong: The matching-line task was intentionally easy and control participants made few errors.

facts.claim: Sacerdote's Dartmouth design randomly paired roommates within 32 housing categories.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because conditional random assignment reduces selection bias, so later differences can be linked more credibly to peer exposure.
facts.commonError: Roommate studies merely compare friends who selected each other.
facts.whyWrong: The first-year pairs were administratively randomized within stated preference groups.

facts.claim: A same-room hotel norm increased towel reuse more than a generic environmental request.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the behavior of people in the identical setting forms a more immediate reference group than an abstract public.
facts.commonError: The broadest possible comparison group creates the strongest norm.
facts.whyWrong: Provincial, context-matched norms performed better in the field experiment.

facts.claim: Social influence operates through both information and peer pressure.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because others' choices may signal hidden facts while their approval or disapproval changes the social cost of dissent.
facts.commonError: Following others always means a person privately believes they are correct.
facts.whyWrong: Compliance can occur to avoid standing apart even when private belief is unchanged.

facts.claim: Descriptive norm messages can increase undesirable behavior among people already performing better than the stated average.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the average supplies a target, so unusually good performers may move toward it from the favorable side.
facts.commonError: Publishing an average can only improve below-average behavior.
facts.whyWrong: The same reference point can pull observations from both directions.

facts.claim: Adding an approval cue can prevent a descriptive-norm boomerang among already efficient households.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the cue communicates that the low-consumption behavior is socially approved rather than merely unusual.
facts.commonError: A smile or approval marker is decorative and cannot alter a numerical comparison.
facts.whyWrong: An injunctive signal changes the meaning of the descriptive information.

facts.claim: The Don't Mess with Texas campaign targeted young men with Texas identity rather than relying only on an anti-litter lecture.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because local pride and admired in-group messengers made proper disposal part of the audience's social identity.
facts.commonError: The slogan was originally a general state-tourism motto.
facts.whyWrong: It was created as an anti-littering campaign for Texas highways.

facts.claim: An informational cascade can persist after later people ignore their private signals and copy earlier public choices.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because once enough visible choices point one way, each follower treats the accumulated behavior as stronger evidence than a private clue.
facts.commonError: A cascade proves that many independent people reached the same conclusion.
facts.whyWrong: Later choices may recycle the same early information rather than add independent evidence.

facts.claim: Norm interventions require local testing because populations can interpret the same message differently.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because reference-group identity, baseline behavior, and cultural meaning determine which social signal is salient.
facts.commonError: A successful social-norm message transfers unchanged to any audience.
facts.whyWrong: The causal mechanism depends on the audience recognizing and valuing the comparison group.
